question.text: Under the Exemption Method of double taxation relief, how is the income treated?

answer.text: Income is taxed in both countries but the residence country provides a refund
Income is taxed in both countries and credit is given for tax paid in the source country
Income is taxed only in the residence country and exempt in the source country
Income is taxed only in the source country and exempt in the residence country

explanation.text: The Logic: International tax treatises and OECD/UN model commentary recognise two principal methods of relieving double taxation. Under the Exemption Method, the income is taxed only in the source country (where it arises) and is fully exempt in the residence country, allocating taxing rights exclusively to the source state. Under the Credit Method, the residence country taxes the income but allows a credit for taxes paid at source. The Exemption Method therefore eliminates double taxation by exempting in residence, not by giving a credit. The Trap: "Taxed in both countries but the residence country provides a refund" and "taxed in both countries and credit is given for tax paid in the source country" both describe the Credit Method, not the Exemption Method. "Taxed only in the residence country and exempt in the source country" reverses the allocation — that would deny source-country taxing rights entirely, which is not how the Exemption Method works. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages reviewed in the audit say DTAAs can avoid double taxation by allocating taxing rights or giving credit, and that in most cases the residence country gives credit for source-country taxes, but the formal "Exemption Method" definition stating that income is taxed only in the source country and exempt in the residence country is not on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general international-taxation method definitions.
